links.note: In 1301 a scribe in Malabar finished a book of Paul's letters for the church. His closing note names the patriarch Yahballaha, 'the Turk', as head of the Church of the East, and Jacob as metropolitan of India. It shows the Indian church honoring its patriarch. But no letter or meeting from these years survives, so the tie rests on this note alone.
links.outcome_considered: A scribe's closing note shows that the patriarch was recognized. It records no council, no split and no changed rule.

links.note: About 1370 Pope Urban V wrote that many heretics lived in Bosnia. He told the archbishops of Split and Dubrovnik to cut off from the church anyone who sheltered them or traded with them. links.outcome_considered: Urban V's letter orders excommunications, but it is a ruling in a letter and no source shows it carried out; Nicholas V's act targets one lord.

prose_changes.old: Lollardy grew out of the teaching of the Oxford theologian John Wycliffe — who attacked church wealth and papal authority, denied transubstantiation, and argued that scripture should be available in English. But it quickly became something much wider than him. Its adherents were mostly ordinary people: weavers, smiths, tailors, wives and widows who owned or shared vernacular scripture, met in one another's houses to read it aloud, and doubted images, pilgrimage and the priest's power over the sacrament. The response was severe. Burning for heresy was made law in England in 1401, Archbishop Arundel's constitutions of 1409 forbade unlicensed translation of scripture into English, and Sir John Oldcastle's failed rising in 1414 made Lollardy treason as well as heresy. After that the movement went underground and survived as scattered household networks into the 1520s. Almost everything we know about those households comes from the records their prosecutors kept — because to convict someone you first had to write down what they said.

prose_changes.old: Jan Hus preached reform in Czech at Prague's Bethlehem Chapel for more than a decade before the Council of Constance burned him as a heretic in 1415. The shock turned a university movement into a national one. Its emblem was the chalice — the insistence that ordinary lay people, and not only priests, should receive the wine at communion. And its program was set out in the Four Articles of Prague in 1420. When crusades were called against Bohemia, the Hussite armies under Jan Žižka and then Prokop the Bald beat them one after another, and in 1436 the Compacts of Basel conceded what no other medieval dissent ever won: legal recognition. Out of that settlement two bodies grew. The Utraquist church held the parishes and, under George of Poděbrady, for a time the crown itself. And from 1457 the Unity of the Brethren, a smaller, stricter, pacifist body formed at Kunvald under the influence of the layman Petr Chelčický, which by 1501 had printed what is often called the first hymnbook in a European vernacular.
